subject: math
title: Greatest Common Factor and Least Common Multiple
seo_title: Grade 6 GCF and LCM Worksheets (BC Curriculum) – Free Math with Answer Key
standard_text: Factors and multiples – greatest common factor and least common multiple
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets for the BC curriculum: factors and multiples, prime and composite numbers, the greatest common factor, the least common multiple, and GCF or LCM word problems. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The GCF is the biggest number that divides all the numbers. The LCM is the first number they all divide into.
key_sub: For 4 and 6: the GCF is 2 and the LCM is 12, not 4 × 6 = 24. Use the GCF for equal groups, rows and pieces, and the LCM for things that repeat or must match, like buses or hot dogs and buns.
body_html:
Factors, multiples and primes

A factor divides a number with no remainder. A multiple is the number times 1, 2, 3, … The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. The multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36, …

A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, …). A composite number has more than two factors. The number 1 is neither.

The greatest common factor (GCF)

A common factor divides two or more numbers. The greatest common factor is the biggest one. List the factors of each number, circle the ones in every list, and pick the greatest.

Example

Find the GCF of 20 and 32.

Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Factors of 32: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Common factors: 1, 2, 4.

Answer: 4

For bigger numbers, use factor trees. Multiply the primes that the numbers share.

The least common multiple (LCM)

A common multiple is in the skip-counting list of every number. The least common multiple is the first one. Count by the biggest number and stop at the first number the others divide into.

Example

Find the LCM of 3, 4 and 6.

Count by 6: 6, 12. 6 is not a multiple of 4, but 12 = 3 × 4 = 4 × 3 = 6 × 2.

Answer: 12

GCF or LCM?

The problem asks…UseExample
The greatest number of identical bags, groups or teamsGCF36 water bottles and 48 granola bars make 12 bags
The biggest equal rows, pieces or squares with nothing left overGCF48 and 36 chairs: rows of 12
When repeating events happen together againLCMBuses every 8 and 12 minutes: 24 minutes
The least number to buy so pack sizes matchLCMHot dogs in 10s, buns in 8s: 40 of each

Check your answer: a GCF is never bigger than the smallest number, and an LCM is never smaller than the biggest number.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Mixing up GCF and LCM: “the GCF of 8 and 12 is 24”24 is the LCM. The GCF is 4
Stopping at any common factor: GCF of 24 and 36 is 6Find the greatest one: 12
Multiplying for the LCM: LCM of 4 and 6 is 2424 is a common multiple, but 12 comes first
Thinking every odd number is prime21 = 3 × 7, so 21 is composite
Calling 1 a prime number1 has only one factor. It is neither prime nor composite
Using only two of three numbersCheck that the answer works for every number

faq.q: How do you find the GCF of two numbers?
faq.a: List the factors of each number and pick the greatest one that is in both lists. For 18 and 24, the common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, so the GCF is 6.

faq.q: How do you find the least common multiple?
faq.a: Count by the bigger number until you reach a number the other one also divides. For 4 and 6, count 6, 12; 12 is a multiple of 4, so the LCM is 12, not 4 × 6 = 24.

faq.q: How do you know whether to use GCF or LCM in a word problem?
faq.a: Use the GCF when you share things into the greatest number of identical groups, or the biggest equal rows or pieces. Use the LCM when events repeat and line up again, or when you buy packs so two amounts match, like hot dogs and buns.

faq.q: Is GCF and LCM in the BC Grade 6 math curriculum?
faq.a: Yes. The BC Grade 6 math curriculum includes factors and multiples, with the greatest common factor and the least common multiple. Students also use prime and composite numbers to find them.

items.q: Which list shows all the factors of 24?
items.e: Find the factor pairs: 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6. So the factors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Include 1 and 24, and don’t forget the pair in the middle.

items.q: Which list shows all the factors of 36?
items.e: Find the factor pairs: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6. So the factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Include 1 and 36, and don’t forget the pair in the middle.

items.q: Which list shows all the factors of 48?
items.e: Find the factor pairs: 1 × 48, 2 × 24, 3 × 16, 4 × 12, 6 × 8. So the factors of 48 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48. Include 1 and 48, and don’t forget the pair in the middle.

items.q: How many factors does 36 have?
items.e: The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. That is 9 factors. 6 × 6 = 36, so 6 is counted only once. Counting 6 twice gives 10, counting pairs gives 5, and leaving out 1 and 36 gives 7.

items.q: How many factors does 60 have?
items.e: The factors of 60 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60. That is 12 factors. Counting pairs gives 6, and leaving out 1 and 60 gives 10. 4 is the number of primes in 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.

items.q: Which number is a factor of 72?
items.e: 18 × 4 = 72, so 18 is a factor of 72. 144 is a multiple of 72, not a factor. 72 ÷ 16 and 72 ÷ 14 have remainders.

items.q: Which number is a factor of 96?
items.e: 12 × 8 = 96, so 12 is a factor of 96. 192 is a multiple of 96, not a factor. 96 ÷ 14 and 96 ÷ 18 have remainders.

items.q: Which number is not a factor of 84?
Which number is not a factor of 90?
Which list shows the first five multiples of 6?
items.e: Multiply 6 by 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first multiple of a number is the number itself, not 0. Count by 6, not by 10. 1, 2, 3, 6 are the factors of 6, not multiples.

items.q: Which list shows the first five multiples of 8?
items.e: Multiply 8 by 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. The first multiple of a number is the number itself, not 0. Count by 8, not by 10. 1, 2, 4, 8 are the factors of 8, not multiples.

items.q: Which number is a multiple of 9?
items.e: 9 × 12 = 108, so 108 is a multiple of 9. 3 is a factor of 9, not a multiple. 89 ÷ 9 and 119 ÷ 9 have remainders. Ending in 9 does not make a number a multiple of 9.

items.q: Which number is a multiple of 8?
items.e: 8 × 12 = 96, so 96 is a multiple of 8. 4 is a factor of 8, not a multiple. 58 ÷ 8 and 108 ÷ 8 have remainders. Ending in 8 does not make a number a multiple of 8.

items.q: Which number is a multiple of 6?
items.e: 6 × 14 = 84, so 84 is a multiple of 6. 3 is a factor of 6, not a multiple. 76 ÷ 6 and 94 ÷ 6 have remainders. Ending in 6 does not make a number a multiple of 6.

items.q: Which number is not a multiple of 7?
Which statement is true?
items.e: 12 × 3 = 36, so 36 is a multiple of 12, and 12 is a factor of 36. A factor is never bigger than the number. A multiple is never smaller.

items.q: These are the factor pairs of 48: 1 × 48, 2 × 24, 3 × ?, 4 × 12, 6 × 8. What is the missing number?
items.e: 3 × 16 = 48, so the missing number is 16. 3 × 15 = 45 and 3 × 17 = 51. 12 is already in the pair 4 × 12.

items.q: This array has 24 counters. Which factor pair of 24 does it show?
items.e: Count the rows and the counters in each row: 3 rows of 8. So the array shows 3 × 8 = 24. 4 × 6 and 2 × 12 are also factor pairs of 24, but they are not this array.

items.q: Which number is a factor of 36 and a multiple of 4?
items.e: 36 = 12 × 3 and 12 = 4 × 3, so 12 is both. 8 is a multiple of 4, but not a factor of 36. 9 and 6 are factors of 36, but not multiples of 4.

items.q: Ava says 3 is a multiple of 12, because 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Is she right?
items.e: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 with no remainder, so 3 is a factor of 12, and 12 is a multiple of 3. The multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36, … They are never smaller than 12.

items.q: Which of these is a prime number?
items.e: 29 has exactly two factors, 1 and 29, so 29 is prime. 27 = 3 × 9, so 27 is not prime. 21 = 3 × 7, so 21 is not prime. 1 has only one factor, so it is not prime.

items.q: Which of these is a prime number?
items.e: 43 has exactly two factors, 1 and 43, so 43 is prime. 49 = 7 × 7, so 49 is not prime. 45 = 3 × 15, so 45 is not prime. 39 = 3 × 13, so 39 is not prime.

items.q: Which of these is a prime number?
items.e: 59 has exactly two factors, 1 and 59, so 59 is prime. 57 = 3 × 19, so 57 is not prime. 51 = 3 × 17, so 51 is not prime. 55 = 5 × 11, so 55 is not prime.

items.q: Which of these is a prime number?
items.e: 71 has exactly two factors, 1 and 71, so 71 is prime. 91 = 7 × 13, so 91 is not prime. 81 = 3 × 27, so 81 is not prime. 77 = 7 × 11, so 77 is not prime.

items.q: Which number is not a prime number?
items.e: 1 has only one factor, so it is not prime. 2, 5 and 7 are prime: each has exactly two factors. 2 is prime, even though it is even.

items.q: Which number is not a prime number?
items.e: 39 = 3 × 13, so 39 is not prime. 2, 41 and 43 are prime: each has exactly two factors. 2 is prime, even though it is even.

items.q: Which number is not a prime number?
items.e: 91 = 7 × 13, so 91 is not prime. 89, 83 and 97 are prime: each has exactly two factors.

items.q: Which of these is a composite number?
items.e: 25 = 5 × 5, so 25 has more than two factors: 25 is composite. 1 is not composite (it has only one factor). 2 and 23 are prime.

items.q: Which of these is a composite number?
items.e: 69 = 3 × 23, so 69 has more than two factors: 69 is composite. 1 is not composite (it has only one factor). 67 and 71 are prime.

items.q: Which statement about the number 1 is true?
c: It is neither prime nor composite
It is both prime and composite
items.e: A prime has exactly two factors and a composite number has more than two. 1 has only one factor, so it is neither.

items.q: How many factors does every prime number have?
items.e: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. More than two factors means composite.

items.q: Simran says 2 is not a prime number because it is even. Is she right?
items.e: The factors of 2 are 1 and 2, so 2 is prime. It is the only even prime: every other even number can be divided by 2, so it is composite.

items.q: Leah says 21 is a prime number because it is odd. Is she right?
items.e: The factors of 21 are 1, 3, 7 and 21. That is more than two factors, so 21 is composite. Many odd numbers are composite: 9, 15, 21, 25, 27, …

items.q: How many prime numbers are there between 20 and 30?
items.e: Test the odd numbers: 21 = 3 × 7, 23 is prime, 25 = 5 × 5, 27 = 3 × 9 and 29 is prime. So there are 2 primes, 23 and 29. 5 counts every odd number.

items.q: How many prime numbers are there between 40 and 50?
items.e: Test the odd numbers: 41, 43 and 47 are prime, 45 = 5 × 9 and 49 = 7 × 7. So there are 3 primes. 5 counts every odd number, and 4 counts 49 as prime.

items.q: Is 51 prime or composite?
c: Prime. It is not in a times table
items.e: 5 + 1 = 6, so 51 is divisible by 3: 51 = 3 × 17. It is composite. 7 × 7 = 49, not 51.

items.q: Which list has only prime numbers?
items.e: 2, 17, 23 and 37 each have exactly two factors, so 2, 17, 23, 37 are all prime. 1 is not prime, 21 = 3 × 7 and 39 = 3 × 13.

items.q: Use the factor tree. What is the prime factorization of 36?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime. The circled numbers are the primes: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. 6 × 6 is not finished, because 6 is not prime. Write a repeated prime every time it appears, and do not write 1 (1 is not prime).

items.q: Use the factor tree. What is the prime factorization of 60?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime. The circled numbers are the primes: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. 6 × 10 is not finished, because 6 and 10 are not prime. Write a repeated prime every time it appears, and do not write 1 (1 is not prime).

items.q: Use the factor tree. What is the prime factorization of 84?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime. The circled numbers are the primes: 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. 7 × 12 is not finished, because 12 is not prime. Write a repeated prime every time it appears, and do not write 1 (1 is not prime).

items.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 12 and 18?
items.e: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The numbers in both lists are 1, 2, 3, 6. Keep 1 and the greatest one.

items.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 24 and 36?
items.e: Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. The numbers in both lists are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Keep 1 and the greatest one.

items.q: The common factors of 18 and 30 are circled. What is the greatest common factor (GCF)?
items.e: The circled numbers are in both lists: 1, 2, 3, 6. The greatest one is 6. 3 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 90 is the least common multiple, not a factor.

items.q: The common factors of 24 and 40 are circled. What is the greatest common factor (GCF)?
items.e: The circled numbers are in both lists: 1, 2, 4, 8. The greatest one is 8. 4 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 120 is the least common multiple, not a factor.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 12 and 16?
items.e: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Common factors: 1, 2, 4. The greatest is 4. 2 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 48 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 18 and 24?
items.e: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6. The greatest is 6. 3 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 72 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 20 and 30?
items.e: Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. Common factors: 1, 2, 5, 10. The greatest is 10. 5 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 60 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 16 and 40?
items.e: Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Factors of 40: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20, 40. Common factors: 1, 2, 4, 8. The greatest is 8. 4 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 80 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 27 and 36?
items.e: Factors of 27: 1, 3, 9, 27. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Common factors: 1, 3, 9. The greatest is 9. 3 is a common factor too, but not the greatest. 108 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 14 and 21?
items.e: Factors of 14: 1, 2, 7, 14. Factors of 21: 1, 3, 7, 21. Common factors: 1, 7. The greatest is 7. 42 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 9 and 16?
items.e: Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Common factors: 1. The greatest is 1. 9 and 16 share no factor except 1, so their GCF is 1.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 15 and 45?
items.e: Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Factors of 45: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45. Common factors: 1, 3, 5, 15. The greatest is 15. 15 divides 45 (15 × 3 = 45), so the smaller number is the GCF. 5 is a common factor, but smaller.

items.q: Use the factor trees. What is the GCF of 36 and 60?
items.e: The trees give 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 and 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Both lists share 2 × 2 × 3. Multiply the shared primes: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. Using each shared prime only once gives 6, which is too small. 180 is the least common multiple.

items.q: Use the factor trees. What is the GCF of 48 and 72?
items.e: The trees give 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Both lists share 2 × 2 × 2 × 3. Multiply the shared primes: 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24. Using each shared prime only once gives 6, which is too small. 144 is the least common multiple.

items.q: What is the GCF of 16, 24 and 36?
items.e: Common factors of 16, 24 and 36: 1, 2, 4. The GCF is 4. The GCF of 16 and 24 alone is 8, but 8 is not a factor of 36. Check all three numbers.

items.q: What is the GCF of 18, 27 and 30?
items.e: Common factors of 18, 27 and 30: 1, 3. The GCF is 3. The GCF of 18 and 27 alone is 9, but 9 is not a factor of 30. Check all three numbers.

items.q: Owen says the GCF of 24 and 36 is 6, because 6 is a factor of both. Is he right?
items.e: 6 is a common factor, but not the greatest. 12 × 2 = 24 and 12 × 3 = 36, so the GCF is 12. 72 is the least common multiple, and 24 is not a factor of 36.

items.q: Ethan says the GCF of 8 and 12 is 24. Is he right?
c: No. 24 is the LCM. The GCF is 4
items.e: 24 is a common multiple. A factor can’t be bigger than the numbers. Factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, 8. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The greatest one in both lists is 4. 2 is a common factor, but not the greatest. 96 is 8 × 12.

items.q: Zara says 9 and 20 have no common factor, so they have no GCF. Is she right?
items.e: 1 is a factor of every whole number, so 1 is always a common factor. 9 = 3 × 3 and 20 = 2 × 2 × 5 share no prime, so the GCF is 1. 180 is their least common multiple.

items.q: Which pair of numbers has a GCF of 6?
items.e: 18 = 6 × 3 and 24 = 6 × 4, and 3 and 4 share no factor, so the GCF of 18 and 24 is 6. The GCF of 12 and 36 is 12, of 2 and 3 is 1 (6 is their LCM), and of 20 and 30 is 10.

items.q: Which numbers in the picture are common multiples of 3 and 5?
items.e: Look for numbers in both rows. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. The common multiples shown are 15, 30. Not only 3 × 5 = 15: 30 is in both rows too.

items.q: Which numbers in the picture are common multiples of 4 and 6?
items.e: Look for numbers in both rows. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36. The common multiples shown are 12, 24, 36. Not only 4 × 6 = 24: 12 and 36 are in both rows too.

items.q: Use the picture. What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 8?
items.e: The first number in both rows is 24, so the least common multiple is 24. 6 × 8 = 48 is a common multiple, but not the least. 2 is the GCF, and 14 is 6 + 8.

items.q: Use the picture. What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 8 and 12?
items.e: The first number in both rows is 24, so the least common multiple is 24. 8 × 12 = 96 is a common multiple, but not the least. 4 is the GCF, and 20 is 8 + 12.

items.q: Which list shows the first three common multiples of 4 and 6?
items.e: The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. The common multiples are the multiples of the LCM: 12, 24, 36. Counting by 4 × 6 = 24 skips 12.

items.q: Which list shows the first three common multiples of 6 and 9?
items.e: The LCM of 6 and 9 is 18. The common multiples are the multiples of the LCM: 18, 36, 54. Counting by 6 × 9 = 54 skips 18.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 3 and 4?
items.e: Count by 4: 4, 8, 12. The first one that is also a multiple of 3 is 12. 3 and 4 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 3 × 4.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 3 and 8?
items.e: Count by 8: 8, 16, 24. The first one that is also a multiple of 3 is 24. 3 and 8 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 3 × 8.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 10?
items.e: Count by 10: 10, 20, 30. The first one that is also a multiple of 6 is 30. 6 × 10 = 60 is a common multiple, but not the least. 2 is the GCF.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 4 and 14?
items.e: Count by 14: 14, 28. The first one that is also a multiple of 4 is 28. 4 × 14 = 56 is a common multiple, but not the least. 2 is the GCF.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 9 and 12?
items.e: Count by 12: 12, 24, 36. The first one that is also a multiple of 9 is 36. 9 × 12 = 108 is a common multiple, but not the least. 3 is the GCF.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 5 and 6?
items.e: Count by 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first one that is also a multiple of 5 is 30. 5 and 6 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 5 × 6.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 10 and 12?
items.e: Count by 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. The first one that is also a multiple of 10 is 60. 10 × 12 = 120 is a common multiple, but not the least. 2 is the GCF.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 15?
items.e: Count by 15: 15, 30. The first one that is also a multiple of 6 is 30. 6 × 15 = 90 is a common multiple, but not the least. 3 is the GCF.

items.q: What is the LCM of 2, 5 and 6?
items.e: Count by the biggest number, 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first one that 2 and 5 also divide is 30. 2 × 5 × 6 = 60 is a common multiple, but not the least. 10 is the LCM of 2 and 5 only. 13 is 2 + 5 + 6.

items.q: What is the LCM of 3, 4 and 6?
items.e: Count by the biggest number, 6: 6, 12. The first one that 3 and 4 also divide is 12. 3 × 4 × 6 = 72 is a common multiple, but not the least. 13 is 3 + 4 + 6.

items.q: Wei says the LCM of 4 and 10 is 40, because 4 × 10 = 40. Is he right?
items.e: Count by 10: 10, 20. 20 = 4 × 5, so the LCM is 20. 40 is a common multiple, but not the least. 2 is the GCF, and 14 is 4 + 10.

items.q: Nadia says the LCM of 6 and 9 is 3. Is she right?
c: No. 3 is the GCF. The LCM is 18
items.e: 3 is the greatest common factor. A multiple can’t be smaller than the numbers. Count by 9: 9, 18. 18 = 6 × 3, so the LCM is 18.

items.q: Chloe says the LCM of 3 and 12 is 12. Is she right?
items.e: 12 = 3 × 4, so 12 is a multiple of both numbers, and no smaller multiple of 12 exists. The LCM is 12. When the bigger number is a multiple of the smaller one, it is the LCM.

items.q: Which pair of numbers has an LCM of 20?
items.e: Count by 10: 10, 20. 20 = 4 × 5, so the LCM of 4 and 10 is 20. The LCM of 2 and 10 is 10, of 4 and 6 is 12, and of 20 and 40 is 40 (20 is their GCF).

sets.title: Word problems: packages, schedules and equal groups

items.q: Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns come in packs of 8. Liam wants the same number of hot dogs and buns for the school barbecue. What is the least number of each he can buy?
items.e: Count by 10: 10, 20, 30, 40. The first one that is also a multiple of 8 is 40. So he buys 40 of each. 10 × 8 = 80 also works, but it is not the least. 2 is the GCF, and 18 is 10 + 8.

items.q: Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns come in packs of 8. Olivia buys the least number of packs so that there is a bun for every hot dog, with none left over. How many packs of buns does she buy?
items.e: The LCM of 10 and 8 is 40, so she needs 40 buns: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 packs. 4 packs is the number of packs of hot dogs (40 ÷ 10). 40 is the number of buns.

items.q: The school has 48 blue chairs and 36 red chairs for an assembly in the gym. Each row has only one colour, and every row has the same number of chairs. What is the greatest number of chairs in each row?
items.e: The row size must divide both 48 and 36. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The GCF is 12. 6 and 4 also work, but they are not the greatest. 144 is the LCM.

items.q: 48 blue chairs and 36 red chairs are set out in rows of 12, and each row has only one colour. How many rows are there?
items.e: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 blue rows and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 red rows. 4 + 3 = 7 rows. 12 is the number of chairs in each row. 14 rows would be rows of 6. 84 is the total number of chairs.

items.q: In Surrey, one bus leaves a stop every 8 minutes and another bus leaves every 12 minutes. Both buses leave at 7:00 a.m. When will they next leave at the same time?
items.e: Count by 12: 12, 24. The first one that is also a multiple of 8 is 24. So they leave together again 24 minutes later, at 7:24 a.m. 8 × 12 = 96 minutes (8:36 a.m.) is not the first time. 20 is 8 + 12, and 4 is the GCF.

items.q: Two whale-watching boats leave Victoria. One leaves every 40 minutes and the other every 60 minutes. Both leave at 9:00 a.m. When will they next leave together?
items.e: Count by 60: 60, 120. The first one that is also a multiple of 40 is 120. 120 minutes is 2 hours, so they leave together at 11:00 a.m. 10:00 a.m. works for the second boat only. 10:40 a.m. uses 40 + 60 = 100 minutes, and 9:20 a.m. uses the GCF, 20.

items.q: Three lights on a float in a Vancouver parade flash every 2, 3 and 5 seconds. They flash together now. In how many seconds will all three next flash together?
items.e: Count by 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. 30 is the first one that 2 and 3 also divide, so the LCM is 30 seconds. 10 is 2 + 3 + 5, 6 works for the first two lights only, and 15 works for the last two only.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Mateo has 36 water bottles and 48 granola bars. He packs identical snack bags with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of bags he can make?
items.e: The number of bags must divide both 36 and 48. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The GCF is 12. 6 also works, but it is not the greatest. 144 is the LCM, and 4 is the number of granola bars in each bag.

items.q: A bulletin board is 60 cm by 84 cm. The class covers it with equal squares of paper, as large as possible, with no gaps or overlaps. What is the side length of each square?
items.e: The side must divide both 60 and 84. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The GCF is 12 cm, which gives 5 rows of 7 squares. 420 is the LCM, and it is bigger than the board.

items.q: Arjun has two ropes for a canoe trip, 54 cm and 90 cm long. He cuts both into pieces of the same length, as long as possible, with nothing left over. How long is each piece?
items.e: The length must divide both 54 and 90. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The GCF is 18 cm: 3 pieces from the first rope and 5 from the second. 270 is the LCM.

items.q: The Grade 6 classes have 24 boys and 30 girls. The teachers make teams for a soccer tournament. Each team has the same number of boys and the same number of girls, and no one is left out. What is the greatest number of teams?
items.e: Find the GCF of 24 and 30. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6. The GCF is 6, so there are 6 teams, each with 4 boys and 5 girls. 3 teams also works, but it is not the greatest. 54 is the total number of students, and 120 is the LCM.

items.q: For a class picnic in Stanley Park, granola bars come in boxes of 6, juice boxes in packs of 8 and apples in bags of 12. Emma wants the same number of each, as few as possible. How many of each does she buy?
items.e: Count by 12: 12, 24. 24 is also a multiple of 6 and of 8, so the LCM is 24. 6 × 8 × 12 = 576 is far more than needed, 26 is 6 + 8 + 12, and 2 is the GCF.

items.q: Hana packs 18 granola bars, 24 apples and 30 juice boxes for a field trip to Grouse Mountain. Every bag must be identical, with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of bags?
items.e: Common factors of 18, 24 and 30: 1, 2, 3, 6. The GCF is 6, so each bag has 3 granola bars, 4 apples and 5 juice boxes. 3 and 2 also work, but they are not the greatest. 360 is the LCM.

items.q: Ryan has hockey practice every 4 days and swimming lessons every 6 days. Both are on April 2. What is the next date when he has both?
items.e: The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, so both happen again 12 days later: April 2 + 12 days = April 14. April 26 uses 4 × 6 = 24 days, April 12 uses 4 + 6 = 10 days, and April 4 uses the GCF, 2.

items.q: Lucas makes the greatest number of identical gift bags from 36 pencils and 60 erasers, with nothing left over. How many erasers are in each bag?
items.e: The GCF of 36 and 60 is 12, so there are 12 bags. 60 ÷ 12 = 5 erasers in each bag (and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 pencils). 12 is the number of bags, and 15 would come from using only 4 bags.

items.q: Orca stickers come in sheets of 6 and salmon stickers come in sheets of 9. Harjot wants the same number of orca and salmon stickers, as few as possible. How many of each does he get?
items.e: Count by 9: 9, 18. The first one that is also a multiple of 6 is 18. That is 3 sheets of orcas and 2 sheets of salmon. 6 × 9 = 54 is not the least, 3 is the GCF, and 15 is 6 + 9.

items.q: A teacher sets out 48 chairs and 60 desks in rows. Every row has the same number of items, and each row has only chairs or only desks. To find the most items in each row, what should you find?
items.e: The row size must divide both numbers, and it must be as big as possible. That is the GCF (12).

items.q: On the SkyTrain platform, one sign flashes every 15 seconds and another every 20 seconds. To find when they next flash together, what should you find?
items.e: The flashes repeat and must line up again, so you need a common multiple: the LCM (60 seconds). 15 × 20 = 300 is a common multiple, but not the first.

items.q: Juice boxes come in packs of 6 and yogurt cups come in packs of 4. Noah says he must buy 24 of each to have the same number. Is he right?
items.e: Count by 6: 6, 12. The first one that is also a multiple of 4 is 12. So 2 packs of juice boxes and 3 packs of yogurt give 12 of each. 24 also works, but it is not the least. 10 is 6 + 4, and 2 is the GCF.

items.q: Jasleen has 16 red beads and 24 blue beads. She wants to make the greatest number of identical bracelets with no beads left over, so she finds the LCM of 16 and 24, which is 48. Is she right?
items.e: Sharing beads into equal groups means the number of bracelets must divide 16 and 24: use the GCF, which is 8. Each bracelet gets 2 red and 3 blue beads. 48 bracelets would need more beads than she has. 4 is a common factor, but not the greatest, and 40 is 16 + 24.
